name: Cryptomnesia
statement: People reproduce words and ideas they have recently heard, believing them to be their own, at rates several times higher than chance.
meaning: Cryptomnesia names a memory error rather than a moral judgement. Something encountered earlier is retrieved without any mark of where it came from, so it arrives feeling like invention. Brown and Murphy set it beside source amnesia and call it an extreme form of the same failure. In source amnesia the item is known to be old and its origin is lost. In cryptomnesia the item feels new. The laboratory version has a fixed three-stage shape. A small group takes turns producing items aloud, from a category or as solutions to a problem. Each person then writes down the items they themselves produced, avoiding everyone else's, and then produces further items that nobody has yet said. A plagiarism is scored when an item someone else generated turns up in either list. What the paradigm measures is a percentage of items written down, over sessions running from ten minutes to a week. That is the whole of what the numbers describe.

origin.who: Alan S. Brown and Dana R. Murphy
origin.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
origin.note: Brown and Murphy write that cryptomnesia had not been directly investigated in a laboratory setting before their three experiments, and they build the generate, recall-own and recall-new sequence the field still uses. The word is much older. Jung's study of so-called occult phenomena, in Constance Long's 1916 translation, calls it the condition that French investigators name cryptomnesia, and Brown and Murphy take their working definition from page 1111 of Taylor's 1965 paper in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

evidence: Brown and Murphy ran three experiments at Southern Methodist University. In the first, 24 students in six groups of four took turns naming members of four categories, four items each per category, 16 items per category in all. They were told not to repeat anything already said. During generation, 10 of the 24 produced an item someone else had given, 13 responses in all, or 3.4% of items and 3.6% after adjusting for repetition opportunities. Recalling their own items, 18 of 24 intruded at least one of someone else's, 28 responses or 7.3% of the total. Generating four new items per category, 17 of 24 did so, 33 words or 8.6%. The reference point was 1.6%, the self-repetition rate Gruenewald and Lockhead recorded for people generating alone. Eight further students generated all 16 items themselves and repeated two items out of 512, a rate of 0.4%. Scrambling those solo protocols into artificial four-person sequences, so that no one could have been monitoring anyone, produced overlap of 17.5%. The observed 3.6% sits between the two. Combining the three tasks of Experiment 1, 38 intrusions came from the person who had spoken immediately before the plagiarist, 22 from the person after and 14 from the non-adjacent person. Experiment 2 tested 64 students and crossed semantic categories against orthographic ones, words starting BE, FO, MA and TH, with four generation patterns. Averaged across the three tasks, plagiarism ran at 13.2% for orthographic material against 7.8% for semantic, and 14.8% when categories were interleaved one item at a time against 8.3% for each of the two blocked patterns. Confidence separated the errors in the recall-own task, where 94.4% of correct items were rated positive and 1.2% a guess, while 25.3% of plagiarised items were rated positive and 48.1% a guess. The same table reverses that in the recall-new task, where 51.4% of plagiarised items were rated positive and 9.9% a guess. In Experiment 3, 21 students worked alone through packs of cards carrying category members, writing an item of their own on every fourth card. Plagiarism was 3.9% during generation, 3.9% in recall-own and 9.8% in recall-new, with one self-plagiarism across all subjects. Experiment 1 produced no self-plagiarism during generation and two in recall-new, though Experiment 2 produced a number of them in the orthographic conditions. Marsh and Bower replaced the group with a computer partner and the categories with Boggle puzzles, and their abstract reports substantially more plagiarism than Brown and Murphy obtained, with retention interval and degree of encoding both moving the rate. Landau and Marsh ran the same Boggle paradigm at the University of Georgia and varied how easily self-generated and computer-generated solutions could be told apart. In their Experiment 1, 42 students either read the computer's solutions intact or were shown them letter by letter and asked to guess. Guessing raised recall-own plagiarism from .46 to .56, F(1,40) = 4.23. In Experiment 2, 40 students played either against the computer or against a human partner who read the computer's solutions aloud. The human partner cut recall-own plagiarism from .50 to .42, F(1,38) = 5.28. Neither manipulation moved the two generative tasks. Generation plagiarism ran .18 against .13 and .17 against .13, generate-new plagiarism .38 against .34 and .42 against .36, and all four of those comparisons fell short of the .05 level. Brédart, Lampinen and Defeldre took the paradigm to Liège with proper names. Forty students worked in same-sex pairs, produced six exemplars each from four name categories, and returned a week later with no instruction to fill every blank. Twelve of the 40 repeated a partner's item during generation, 14 responses or 1.5% of items. Confidence on a five-point scale was 4.26 for correct recalls, 2.53 for plagiarised ones and 2.50 for items nobody had said, and 47.9% of the plagiarised responses still drew a rating of 3 or better. Words that somebody plagiarised were recalled at .33 when the partner had produced them and .06 when nobody had, t(33) = 6.54. Their second experiment ran 42 students through a memory characteristics questionnaire instead. It scored 702 responses, 500 correct, 97 plagiarised and 105 intrusions of items nobody had said. About half the plagiarised ones carried a top rating on at least one qualitative characteristic. Bink, Marsh, Hicks and Howard attributed traffic-safety ideas to traffic planners or to college freshmen. Their abstract reports more plagiarism of the credible source in Experiments 1 and 2, with no matching difference in explicit memory for who said what. The difference was gone in Experiment 3, where participants worked out the implications of the ideas at study. Stark and Perfect tested repeated elaboration at Plymouth. Sixty-four students generated alternate uses for a brick, a button, a paperclip and a shoe, and 55 of them returned for the test a week later. Ideas were left alone, elaborated on day one, on day three, or on both days. Imagining an idea left recall-own plagiarism near control, at 10.4% of ideas output for control against 12.5%, 16.3% and 16.0%. Writing three improvements to it raised plagiarism from 16.0% for control ideas to 27.3%, 26.0% and 48.0%. In raw counts, twice-improved ideas were plagiarised over 13 times as often as control ideas. Plagiarism in the generate-new task did not follow the same pattern. Perfect and Stark then asked whether the improvement effect runs on self-relevance. They tested 30 and 32 students and analysed 27 and 29, the rest having missed the second session. Experiment 1 again used alternate uses for common objects, and Experiment 2 replaced them with ideas for improving the participants' university course, its facilities, the city centre and student life. A quarter of each person's ideas were left alone, a quarter imagined, a quarter improved for the participant's own use and a quarter improved for an older adult. As a proportion of ideas output in the recall-own task, control ideas were plagiarised 15.6% and 26.8% of the time across the two experiments, and imagined ideas 15.6% and 21.7%. Ideas improved for the participant's own use ran at 36.6% and 41.5%, and ideas improved for someone else at 36.2% and 41.1%. Outside the laboratory, Defeldre asked 202 people to recall an episode of inadvertent plagiarism from their own past. The abstract reports that such episodes occur in real life across various types of activity, and that same-sex plagiarism occurred more often than opposite-sex.

examples.tag: The idea that came to you in the shower
examples.text: A fix for a process arrives fully formed on a Tuesday morning and you put it to the meeting as your own. A colleague raised it three weeks earlier at the end of a long call. You are not lying, because nothing about the thought arrived carrying a date.

A songwriter hums a phrase, finds it good and finds it new. It is the chorus of something that played twice in a car park a fortnight ago. The experience of invention and the experience of recall are the same experience when the mark of pastness is missing.

examples.tag: The anecdote told back to its owner
examples.text: Someone repeats a story about a train at a dinner party, and the person opposite is the one who told it to her. The failure is not that she forgot who said it. It is that the story felt like hers to tell.

replication.headline: Four research groups in three countries have obtained the effect in the three-stage paradigm, using category exemplars, word puzzles, proper names and creative ideas.
replication.detail: Brédart, Lampinen and Defeldre are the cleanest independent repeat that could be read in full. Working in Liège rather than Texas, with proper names rather than category exemplars, in pairs rather than groups of four, and across a week rather than ten minutes, they obtained plagiarism in both experiments. They also dropped the instruction that had drawn the sharpest methodological objection to Brown and Murphy, which is that participants must write something on every blank, and the errors survived it. A word somebody plagiarised was recalled at .33 when the partner had produced it and .06 when nobody had, which is the check that separates plagiarism from coincidence. Marsh and Bower moved the paradigm to a Boggle puzzle and a computer partner and report more plagiarism than Brown and Murphy found, though only their abstract was reached. Landau and Marsh, Bink and colleagues, Stark and Perfect at Plymouth, and Hollins and colleagues have each obtained plagiarism in the paradigm while manipulating something else. The one published contradiction inside the literature is about a moderator rather than about the effect. Perfect, Defeldre, Elliman and Dehon ran three experiments with younger and older participants and found no age-related increase in plagiarism, which they state stands against the single previous demonstration of one. Older adults instead intruded more items nobody had generated. The idea-improvement effect, in which writing improvements to someone else's idea roughly doubles the rate at which it is later recalled as one's own, has been obtained repeatedly, and every report of it located here comes from Perfect, Stark and their Plymouth colleagues. A search on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, DataCite, OpenAlex, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall and the open web found no meta-analysis of cryptomnesia, and no multi-site or preregistered replication of any part of it.

study.cite: Brédart, S., Lampinen, J. M., & Defeldre, A.-C. (2003). Phenomenal characteristics of cryptomnesia. Memory, 11(1), 1-11.

limits: The paradigm bounds the claim tightly. It measures what happens to single words or one-line ideas heard minutes or days earlier, usually in a task that forces an output on every blank line, among strangers who have no stake in the answer. It says nothing about how often a novelist, a songwriter or a researcher reproduces someone else's work, and it cannot say so, because no laboratory can run that study. Brown and Murphy's own choice of baseline is a judgement call they discuss at length: 1.6% comes from a different task in a different laboratory, and the solo-generation control they added returned 0.4%. Their Experiment 1 had 24 participants. The Plymouth studies lose people between generation and test, and the figures above rest on the smaller number. Stark and Perfect tested 64 and analysed 55, and Perfect and Stark tested 30 and 32 and analysed 27 and 29. Searches on 21 September 2026 ran across Crossref, DataCite, OpenAlex, PubMed, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, CORE, OpenAIRE, the Internet Archive, the Caselaw Access Project and the open web. Brown and Murphy was read in full from a scan hosted by the University of Warwick. Landau and Marsh, and Stark and Perfect, were read in full from archived copies of the publisher's own PDFs, which Springer now answers with a client challenge rather than a paywall. Perfect and Stark's 2012 article is open access and was read in full. Brédart, Lampinen and Defeldre was read from the author postprint deposited at ORBi, so its wording may differ from the published article, which is closed at the publisher. Perfect, Defeldre, Elliman and Dehon is indexed as open, and the file at ORBi is a two-page author manuscript carrying the title page and the abstract and nothing else. Seven papers were not obtained in full. Marsh and Bower, Bink and colleagues, Stark, Perfect and Newstead, and Perfect, Field and Jones are quoted here only from their PubMed abstracts, and are closed at their publishers. Defeldre is quoted only from the abstract OpenAlex carries. Marsh, Landau and Hicks has no abstract at PubMed, Crossref or OpenAlex, and nothing on this page rests on it. Taylor's 1965 paper carries no abstract at PubMed and is closed at Cambridge. Hollins and colleagues is indexed as open by Semantic Scholar, the Plymouth author manuscript it points at has a handle that no longer resolves, and the repository holding it answers with a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall. The archived snapshot of that record page carries the abstract but not the file. Louisa-Jayne Stark's Plymouth thesis is the same case, with a readable record page and abstract and a PDF behind the same challenge. Perfect and Stark's 2008 chapter and Kreuz's 2026 chapter sit in books, and neither text was reached. Tenpenny, Keriazakos, Lew and Phelan's 1998 paper is named by later papers as the source of the objection that Brown and Murphy forced a response on every blank, and it was not obtained. Per-condition percentages for Marsh and Bower's immediate and delayed conditions circulate widely and appear in no source reached here, so they are left out.
misreadings: The first misreading is scale. A finding that 8.6% of words on a worksheet were borrowed is not a finding that some proportion of books are, and the laboratory literature will not support an accusation against any actual author. The second is confidence, and it runs in both directions. Brown and Murphy's participants were unsure of what they plagiarised while recalling their own items: 48.1% of those items were rated a guess and 25.3% positive, against 94.4% positive for items they really had produced. The same table reverses in the recall-new task, where 51.4% of plagiarised items were rated positive and 9.9% a guess. Brédart, Lampinen and Defeldre pushed on this. Dropping the instruction to fill every blank, they still found confidence lower for plagiarised items, 2.53 against 4.26 on a five-point scale, and reported that 47.9% of plagiarised items drew a rating of 3 or better. Low average confidence is not an absence of confidence. The third misreading is the George Harrison case. Judge Owen held in Bright Tunes Music Corp. v. Harrisongs Music, Ltd. that My Sweet Lord infringed He's So Fine. He wrote that he did not believe Harrison had used the earlier music deliberately, and that the infringement was 'no less so even though subconsciously accomplished'. The finding cut both ways. Assessing damages in 1981, the same judge attributed $1,599,987 of the song's earnings to the borrowed music, and wrote that had he found deliberate plagiarism he would have awarded the entire earnings of My Sweet Lord. The case is a ruling on liability, not a measurement of anyone's memory, and it does not establish that cryptomnesia occurred. Two stock anecdotes do have primary sources, contrary to their reputation. Helen Keller devoted a chapter of The Story of My Life to 'The Frost King', which she was writing in the autumn of 1891 and which brought the trouble of the winter of 1892. Margaret Canby's 'The Frost Fairies' had appeared before Keller was born. She was brought before a court of investigation of the teachers and officers of the Perkins Institution, and her teacher was asked to leave her. Keller adds that Anagnos later said the panel was eight people, four of whom thought she had known the Canby story, and that he voted with the other four. Jung printed the Zarathustra passage in parallel columns against Kerner's Blätter aus Prevorst, volume four, page 57, and named the log of the ship Sphinx of 1686 that it came from. What the Jung anecdote rests on is thinner than the parallel text suggests. His only evidence that Nietzsche ever read Kerner is what the poet's sister told him in reply to his inquiry, that Nietzsche took Kerner up between the ages of twelve and fifteen and certainly never afterwards. Last, misattributing a source is a different error with its own entry, at 239, which draws the contrast in full. Cryptomnesia requires that the mark of pastness be gone. False memory, at 35, builds an event that never happened, and source bias, at 329, is about how a source's standing moves belief.

sources.text: Brown, A. S., & Murphy, D. R. (1989). Cryptomnesia: Delineating inadvertent plagiarism. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 15(3), 432-442. Read in full from a scan hosted by the University of Warwick; the source for every figure in the first half of the evidence section.

Brédart, S., Lampinen, J. M., & Defeldre, A.-C. (2003). Phenomenal characteristics of cryptomnesia. Memory, 11(1), 1-11. Read in full from the author postprint deposited at ORBi, the University of Liège repository; the published article is closed and the two versions were not compared. The source for the confidence ratings, the conditional-probability check and the memory characteristics questionnaire result.

Marsh, R. L., & Bower, G. H. (1993). Eliciting cryptomnesia: Unconscious plagiarism in a puzzle task. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 19(3), 673-688. Abstract read at PubMed. The full text is closed at the publisher, and no open copy was found on 21 September 2026 at Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, CORE or the Internet Archive; the per-condition rates were not obtained.

Landau, J. D., & Marsh, R. L. (1997). Monitoring source in an unconscious plagiarism paradigm. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 4(2), 265-270. Read in full from an archived copy of the publisher's PDF, which Springer itself now answers with a client challenge rather than a paywall; the source for the two Boggle experiments and their Table 1.

Marsh, R. L., Landau, J. D., & Hicks, J. L. (1997). Contributions of inadequate source monitoring to unconscious plagiarism during idea generation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 23(4), 886-897. Listed because it exists and is cited throughout this literature. No abstract is carried by PubMed, Crossref or OpenAlex, the text is closed at the publisher, and nothing on this page rests on it.

Bink, M. L., Marsh, R. L., Hicks, J. L., & Howard, J. D. (1999). The credibility of a source influences the rate of unconscious plagiarism. Memory, 7(3), 293-308. Abstract read at PubMed; the full text is closed at the publisher.

Perfect, T. J., & Stark, L.-J. (2012). Unconscious plagiarism in recall: Attribution to the self, but not for self-relevant reasons. Europe's Journal of Psychology, 8(2), 275-283. Open access and read in full; the source for the idea-improvement percentages and for the recruited and analysed sample sizes.

Stark, L.-J., Perfect, T. J., & Newstead, S. (2005). When elaboration leads to appropriation: Unconscious plagiarism in a creative task. Memory, 13(6), 561-573. Abstract read at PubMed; the full text is closed at the publisher. Crossref and OpenAlex date it 2004 against the journal's 2005 issue.

Stark, L.-J., & Perfect, T. J. (2008). The effects of repeated idea elaboration on unconscious plagiarism. Memory & Cognition, 36(1), 65-73. Read in full from an archived copy of the publisher's PDF, which Springer itself now answers with a client challenge rather than a paywall; the source for the repeated-elaboration percentages and for the 64 tested against 55 analysed.

Perfect, T. J., Field, I., & Jones, R. (2009). Source credibility and idea improvement have independent effects on unconscious plagiarism errors in recall and generate-new tasks. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 35(1), 267-274. Abstract read at PubMed, which reports the double dissociation; the full text is closed at the publisher.

Perfect, T. J., Defeldre, A.-C., Elliman, R., & Dehon, H. (2011). No evidence of age-related increases in unconscious plagiarism during free recall. Memory, 19(5), 514-528. Abstract read at PubMed and confirmed against the author manuscript at ORBi, which runs to two pages holding the title page and the abstract and no results.

Hollins, T. J., Lange, N., Dennis, I., & Longmore, C. A. (2016). Social influences on unconscious plagiarism and anti-plagiarism. Memory, 24(7), 884-902. Abstract read at PubMed. Semantic Scholar lists the Plymouth author manuscript as open, its handle no longer resolves, and PEARL answers with a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall; the file is absent from the archived snapshot of the record page.

Defeldre, A.-C. (2005). Inadvertent plagiarism in everyday life. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 19(8), 1033-1040. Abstract read at OpenAlex; the full text is closed at the publisher. The abstract gives the sample of 202 and the same-sex finding, and no breakdown of how many participants recalled an episode.

Stark, L.-J. (2005). The effects of idea elaboration on unconscious plagiarism. Thesis, University of Plymouth. Eleven experiments. The record page and abstract were read at PEARL and the metadata confirmed at DataCite; the thesis PDF sits behind a Cloudflare challenge rather than a paywall, and nothing here rests on it.

Tenpenny, P. L., Keriazakos, M. S., Lew, G. S., & Phelan, T. P. (1998). In search of inadvertent plagiarism. The American Journal of Psychology, 111(4), 529. Named here because Brédart and colleagues and Stark and Perfect both cite it, the first for the objection that Brown and Murphy forced a response on every blank. Metadata verified at Crossref; the paper itself was not obtained and carries no abstract at PubMed or OpenAlex.

Taylor, F. K. (1965). Cryptomnesia and plagiarism. British Journal of Psychiatry, 111(480), 1111-1118. The definition Brown and Murphy quote. Metadata verified at Crossref; PubMed carries no abstract and the paper itself was not read.

Kreuz, R. J. (2026). Unconscious plagiarism. In Strikingly Similar, pp. 60-88. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Listed as the most recent book-length treatment. Cambridge Core returned only navigation and a service-disruption notice on 21 September 2026, and nothing on this page rests on it.

Bright Tunes Music Corp. v. Harrisongs Music, Ltd., 420 F. Supp. 177 (S.D.N.Y. 1976), Owen J., decided 31 August 1976. Full opinion read from the Caselaw Access Project scan of the Federal Supplement.

ABKCO Music, Inc. v. Harrisongs Music, Ltd., 508 F. Supp. 798 (S.D.N.Y. 1981), Owen J., decided 19 February 1981. The damages ruling, read from the Caselaw Access Project scan; the source for the $1,599,987 figure and for the note that deliberate plagiarism would have carried the whole of the song's earnings.

Keller, H. (1903). The Story of My Life. Chapter 14 gives her own account of writing 'The Frost King', of the court of investigation that followed, and of what Anagnos said about it afterwards. Read in full at Project Gutenberg.

Jung, C. G. (1916). On the psychology and pathology of so-called occult phenomena. In Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology, ed. C. E. Long, pp. 86-89. London: Bailliere, Tindall and Cox. The attribution of the term to French investigators, the parallel columns setting Thus Spoke Zarathustra against Kerner's Blätter aus Prevorst, and the report of what Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche said in reply to Jung's inquiry. Read from the Cornell scan at the Internet Archive.
